lesson.title: Naming the Number: The Definite Integral as Net Signed Area
lesson.summary: The definite integral is simply the name given to the limiting value of a Riemann sum, and because the sum can include negative contributions, it measures net signed area rather than plain area.
lesson.body:
The previous chapter showed that as the rectangles in a Riemann sum get thinner and more numerous, the sum settles onto one exact number. That number deserves a name, because it shows up constantly once you start asking questions about accumulated quantities: total distance from a velocity, total charge from a current, total revenue from a rate of sales. The definite integral of f from a to b is defined to be exactly that limiting value, the number that the Riemann sums converge to as the number of subintervals grows without bound and their width shrinks to 0. Nothing new is being invented here. The definite integral is not a separate idea bolted onto the limit of a Riemann sum, it is that limit, given a name so it can be used in formulas and reasoning without rewriting the whole limiting process every time.

One detail matters enormously and trips up almost every student the first time they see it: the definite integral measures signed area, not plain area. If f(x) is negative on part of the interval, the rectangles built on that part have negative height in the sum, so they subtract from the total rather than adding to it. The definite integral therefore reports net area: area above the x axis counts as positive, area below counts as negative, and the two can cancel. This is not a flaw in the definition, it is exactly what makes the definite integral useful for tracking things like displacement, where moving backward should subtract from your total rather than adding more distance on top.

Here is a worked example that shows the cancellation directly. Let f(x) = x on the interval [-1, 2]. Break the region into two pieces at x = 0. On [-1, 0], the graph of f is a line from (-1, -1) to (0, 0), lying entirely below the x axis. That piece is a triangle with base 1 and height 1, so its area is 1/2, but since it lies below the axis it contributes -1/2 to the signed total. On [0, 2], the graph runs from (0, 0) to (2, 2), lying entirely above the axis. That piece is a triangle with base 2 and height 2, so its area is 1/2 times 2 times 2 = 2, contributing +2. Adding the two signed pieces gives -1/2 + 2 = 3/2. So the definite integral of x from -1 to 2 equals 3/2, even though the plain, unsigned area enclosed by the graph and the axis on that interval is larger, 1/2 + 2 = 5/2. The difference between those two numbers is exactly the point: the definite integral tracks net accumulation, with the part below the axis working against the part above it.

Keep this signed nature in mind going forward. Every property of the definite integral, including how it behaves under the fundamental theorem later in this chapter sequence, respects this bookkeeping of positive and negative contributions rather than treating everything as plain, unsigned area.
